topic: Frontier Lab · Phase 2: Scaling Laws & Inference

questions.title: Kaplan vs Chinchilla scaling laws
questions.prompt: Kaplan et al. and Chinchilla both fit scaling laws for LLM pretraining but reached different conclusions about how to split a compute budget between model size and data. Explain what Chinchilla corrected and how the IsoFLOP method found it.
probes: Why did Kaplan's methodology bias toward oversized models?
What breaks if you train a Kaplan-sized model on Chinchilla-optimal data instead?
criteria: Kaplan favored large N, undertrained
Chinchilla ~20 tokens/param
IsoFLOP: fix C, vary N, find loss-minimizing N
both N and D scale ~C^0.5
Kaplan's LR schedule/warmup confound

no_hire.answer: Chinchilla showed bigger models are better, so you should just make the model as large as possible.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Backwards. Misses that Chinchilla argued for smaller models trained on more data, and gives no method.

weak_hire.answer: Kaplan's scaling laws said to mostly grow model size and undertrain on data. Chinchilla found this was wrong and that you should scale data roughly in proportion to parameters, about 20 tokens per parameter, and it trained a smaller model on more tokens than GPT-3-era models and beat them.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Knows the headline result and the 20:1 ratio, but no explanation of why Kaplan was wrong or how Chinchilla derived the number.

hire.answer: Kaplan et al. fit N and D scaling separately and used a fixed LR schedule length across runs, which biased their fit toward allocating most compute to parameters and undertraining on data. Chinchilla instead ran IsoFLOP sweeps: for several fixed compute budgets C, train models of many sizes N until convergence, plot loss vs N, and read off the N (and implied D=C/6N) that minimizes loss at each C. Fitting a power law across these minima gives N_opt and D_opt both scaling roughly as C^0.5, and the resulting D/N ratio is about 20 tokens per parameter, versus Kaplan's much higher N/D allocation.
hire.interviewer_note: Correct methodology and root cause (LR schedule confound), states the C^0.5 scaling. Solid staff-level answer.

strong_hire.answer: Kaplan's laws (approach 1: fixed-shape single fits) held training length fixed in the LR schedule across different N, so smaller-N/larger-D configurations were systematically undertrained mid-schedule, making the data underweighted in the fit and pushing the optimal allocation toward huge N. Chinchilla used three complementary approaches, most cited being IsoFLOP profiles (approach 2): for a set of fixed C, sweep N with each run using a cosine schedule tuned to its own token budget so every point is fairly converged, then fit a parabola to loss vs log N at each C to locate the minimum. Across many C, N_opt(C) and D_opt(C) both fit power laws with exponent close to 0.5, giving D_opt/N_opt ~ 20. Practically this means C=6ND is the constraint, loss L(N,D) = E + A/N^a + B/D^b is the objective, and the IsoFLOP minima trace out the (N,D) frontier that minimizes L for fixed C. The correction matters operationally: it shows most contemporaneous LLMs (GPT-3, Gopher, MT-NLG) were oversized and undertrained, and a smaller model trained compute-optimally (Chinchilla, 70B/1.4T tokens vs Gopher 280B/300B tokens) can strictly dominate on loss at equal or lower FLOPs. I'd also flag the caveat Chinchilla itself notes: the exponents are fit on a specific data distribution and can shift with data quality/repetition, so I'd re-fit on my own IsoFLOP sweep rather than trust the constant 20 blindly.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Names the LR-schedule confound precisely, describes IsoFLOP methodology and the parabola-fit-per-budget mechanism, gives the full loss functional form, and adds a production caveat about re-fitting. Principal-level.

questions.title: Prefill vs decode and the memory wall
questions.prompt: Prove that single-token autoregressive decode is bound by moving weights from HBM to SRAM rather than by compute, and contrast this with prefill.
probes: What is arithmetic intensity and why does it land near 1 for decode?
What GPU spec ratio (FLOPs/s vs bytes/s) tells you whether you're compute- or memory-bound?
criteria: arithmetic intensity = FLOPs / bytes moved
decode: 1 token needs full weight read, ~O(1) FLOP per weight per token
roofline: intensity << FLOPs/byte ratio of GPU -> memory bound
prefill processes many tokens per weight read -> compute bound
consequence: decode throughput scales with batch, not raw FLOPs

no_hire.answer: Decode is slow because generating tokens one at a time is slower than processing a whole prompt at once.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Restates the symptom with no mechanism, no arithmetic intensity, no proof.

weak_hire.answer: During decode you generate one token per forward pass, so you have to load all the model weights from memory for each token, which is expensive relative to how little compute you actually do. Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel so it does much more compute per weight load and is compute-bound.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct intuition and direction of the effect, but no quantitative argument, no arithmetic intensity or roofline reasoning.

hire.answer: Define arithmetic intensity I = FLOPs done / bytes moved from HBM. For a matmul of a weight matrix W (shape d_in x d_out) against a batch of B token-vectors, FLOPs ~ 2*B*d_in*d_out and bytes moved ~ (d_in*d_out) for the weights (loaded once) plus O(B*(d_in+d_out)) for activations; for B=1 (single-token decode) I ~ 2*d_out (independent of the weight size, roughly O(1) in the useful sense that it doesn't grow with model size) which is far below the GPU's FLOPs/byte ratio (e.g. A100: ~312 TFLOPs bf16 / ~2TB/s HBM ~ 156 FLOPs/byte). Since I << that ratio, the GPU sits idle waiting on HBM bandwidth: decode is memory-bound. Prefill with sequence length L pushes I up by roughly a factor of L (B effectively becomes L tokens processed against the same weight load), crossing into compute-bound territory once L is large enough.
hire.interviewer_note: Gets the roofline argument, the intensity formula, and a concrete GPU number. Strong quantitative answer.

strong_hire.answer: Roofline model: a kernel is memory-bound if its arithmetic intensity I = FLOPs/bytes is less than the GPU's ridge point I* = peak FLOPs/s divided by peak HBM bandwidth (e.g. A100 bf16: ~312e12/2e12 ~ 156 FLOPs/byte; H100 is similar order). For a linear layer W in R^{d_in x d_out} applied to a batch of B tokens: FLOPs = 2*B*d_in*d_out, bytes moved (weight-dominated, since weights >> activations for large d) approx = 2*d_in*d_out (bf16), so I(B) = B (independent of layer width!). At decode, B=1 (per-sequence) so I=1, which is orders of magnitude below the ridge point of ~150-200 on modern GPUs -- proof that decode sits deep in the memory-bound region regardless of model size, and adding FLOPs (bigger d_in, d_out) does not change I=B, only bytes moved. Prefill processes B=L prompt tokens against the same one-time weight load, so I=L; once L exceeds the ridge point (~150-200 tokens, roughly true for most real prompts) prefill crosses into compute-bound. The practical consequence: decode throughput is fixed by HBM bandwidth divided by model byte-size (tokens/s ~ BW / bytes_per_token_pass), which is why the only lever for decode throughput is batching multiple sequences together to raise effective B (and thus I) toward the ridge point -- this is exactly why continuous batching and larger batch sizes give near-linear throughput gains until you hit the ridge point, after which you become compute-bound and batching stops helping for free (KV cache growth then becomes the binding memory constraint). This is also the core justification for speculative decoding and chunked prefill: both are techniques to raise the effective arithmetic intensity of the decode phase.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Derives I(B)=B as a width-independent invariant, cites the actual GPU ridge point, connects to why batching helps only up to the ridge, and links to speculative decoding/chunked prefill as intensity-raising techniques. Systems-mastery depth.

questions.title: Batching economics and the KV cache tradeoff
questions.prompt: Explain why increasing batch size improves decode throughput, and why it can't be increased without bound. What's the tension with the KV cache?
probes: Write down how KV cache memory scales with batch size and context length.
At what point does increasing batch size stop helping throughput?
criteria: larger batch amortizes one weight load across more tokens
raises arithmetic intensity toward compute-bound
KV cache size scales linearly with batch * seq_len * layers * heads * head_dim
HBM capacity caps max batch, not just bandwidth
beyond ridge point, compute becomes the bottleneck

no_hire.answer: Bigger batches are always faster, so you should use as large a batch as the GPU allows.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Ignores the actual constraint and the tradeoff the question asks about.

weak_hire.answer: Batching lets you process multiple requests' tokens together per weight load, which is more efficient and raises throughput. But the KV cache for every sequence in the batch has to be stored in GPU memory, so a bigger batch needs more memory, and eventually you run out.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: States the tradeoff qualitatively but no formula for KV cache growth and no mention of the compute-bound crossover.

hire.answer: One weight load from HBM is shared across all B sequences in a decode step, so FLOPs done per byte of weight moved scales with B, raising arithmetic intensity and throughput -- this is why decode throughput scales close to linearly with batch size while still memory-bound. But KV cache memory = 2 (K and V) * batch * seq_len * num_layers * num_heads * head_dim * bytes_per_element, which grows linearly in batch size and in context length, competing with weights for the same fixed HBM. Past some batch size, either you exceed available memory or arithmetic intensity crosses the GPU's ridge point and you become compute-bound, so throughput growth flattens.
hire.interviewer_note: Correct KV cache formula, correct amortization logic, and correct dual-limit reasoning. Strong.

strong_hire.answer: Decode throughput per step is upper-bounded by min(compute-bound throughput, memory-bandwidth-bound throughput); increasing batch B raises arithmetic intensity I(B)=B (weight bytes amortized across B sequences), moving you along the bandwidth-bound regime with throughput growing ~linearly in B until I approaches the GPU's ridge point (~150-200 for A100/H100-class bf16), after which the FLOPs term dominates and further batching gives diminishing returns. The binding constraint before you even reach the compute ridge is usually HBM capacity: KV_bytes = 2 * B * L * n_layers * n_heads * head_dim * dtype_size, which for a 70B-class model with long context (say L=8k) can exceed the weight memory itself, so max feasible B is set by (HBM_total - weights_bytes) / KV_bytes_per_sequence. This is the fundamental batch-size vs context-length tradeoff: doubling context length halves the max batch you can serve, and vice versa. Production mitigations: PagedAttention to eliminate KV fragmentation waste and raise effective max B; multi-query/grouped-query attention (fewer KV heads) to shrink KV_bytes_per_sequence by a large constant factor, directly buying more headroom for batch size; KV cache quantization (FP8/INT8) for another ~2-4x; and disaggregated prefill/decode serving so decode-pool memory isn't shared with prefill's transient activation memory. The right way to reason about capacity planning is jointly solving the batch-vs-context frontier against a fixed HBM budget, not treating batch size as a free knob.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Full roofline-aware amortization argument, exact KV formula with capacity-constraint solve, GQA/quantization/PagedAttention as concrete production levers, and the batch-vs-context frontier framing. Staff/principal serving-economics depth.

questions.title: Mixture-of-Experts fundamentals
questions.prompt: Explain how a Mixture-of-Experts layer works: the gating function, top-k routing, and the distinction between active and total parameters.
probes: Why does MoE let you scale total parameters without scaling FLOPs per token?
What happens to the softmax gate values for experts that aren't in the top-k?
criteria: router/gate produces per-expert score for each token
top-k selection, e.g. k=2 of E experts
output = weighted sum of selected experts' outputs, gate weights renormalized
active params (used per token) vs total params (all experts resident)
compute scales with active params, memory with total params

no_hire.answer: MoE has several expert networks and the model picks whichever expert is best at answering the question, like consulting different specialists.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Analogy without mechanism; no gating math, no top-k, no active/total distinction.

weak_hire.answer: An MoE layer replaces a single feedforward block with several expert feedforward blocks plus a small router network. For each token, the router scores the experts and picks the top few, and only those experts process that token. This means the model can have many more total parameters than a dense model while each token only uses a fraction of them.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct high-level mechanism and the active-vs-total intuition, but no formula for the gate, no renormalization detail, no compute accounting.

hire.answer: The router computes logits g(x) = W_r x for each of E experts, takes a softmax, and keeps only the top-k values (typically k=1 or 2), renormalizing those k softmax weights to sum to 1; all other experts get weight 0 and are not computed for that token. The layer output is sum over the top-k experts of (gate_weight_i * Expert_i(x)). Active parameters are the router plus the k experts actually invoked per token, which determines FLOPs/token; total parameters are the router plus all E experts, which determines memory footprint. This is the key lever: e.g. 8 experts with k=2 gives ~4x more total parameters than a dense model at roughly the same FLOPs/token as a 2-expert-wide dense layer.
hire.interviewer_note: Full gating formula with renormalization, correct active/total split with a concrete ratio example. Solid.

strong_hire.answer: Formally, for token x: gate logits g = W_r x in R^E, probabilities p = softmax(g), then TopK(p, k) zeroes out all but the k largest entries and (in most implementations, e.g. Switch/GShard/Mixtral) renormalizes the surviving k weights to sum to 1 so the output is a proper convex combination: y = sum_{i in TopK} (p_i / sum_{j in TopK} p_j) * FFN_i(x). Active parameters/token = router params + k * (params per expert); compute/token scales only with active params, so FLOPs/token stays roughly constant as you add more experts (holding k fixed) -- this is the core value proposition, decoupling model capacity (total params, which correlates with representational/memorization capacity) from inference compute cost. Total parameters = router + E * (params per expert), and all E experts must be resident in memory regardless of routing, so memory scales with E even though compute doesn't. Concretely, Mixtral 8x7B has ~47B total params but only ~13B active per token (2 of 8 experts plus shared attention/embedding params), so it trains/infers at roughly a 13B dense model's FLOP cost while having the representational capacity closer to a much larger dense model. The important subtlety: because gradients only flow through the k selected experts for a given token, the effective training signal per expert is sparser than a dense FFN of equivalent total size, which is why routing quality (addressed by load balancing) directly determines how well that extra total capacity gets utilized.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Exact gating formula with renormalization, precise active/total parameter formulas, a concrete real-model number (Mixtral), and connects sparsity to training-signal-per-expert as a bridge to the load-balancing question. Research-engineer depth.

questions.title: MoE load balancing and its effect on scaling
questions.prompt: Explain the load-balancing problem in MoE training: expert capacity limits, token dropping, and the auxiliary load-balancing loss. Then explain why MoE models are more data-hungry than dense models of equal active-parameter count -- i.e. why their scaling law has a different exponent.
probes: What exactly does the auxiliary load-balancing loss penalize, mathematically?
Why would insufficient data make an MoE model underperform a dense model with the same active FLOPs?
criteria: routing collapse: router favors a few experts, positive feedback loop
expert capacity factor caps tokens per expert per batch, overflow tokens dropped/rerouted
aux loss penalizes deviation from uniform expert usage (importance x load product)
dropped tokens = wasted compute / degraded quality
MoE needs more tokens per active-param to reach its capacity potential -> different D-scaling exponent than dense

no_hire.answer: Sometimes one expert gets too many tokens and others get too few, so you balance them out during training.
no_hire.interviewer_note: States the symptom with no mechanism (capacity, aux loss) and doesn't touch the data-scaling question at all.

weak_hire.answer: Without intervention, the router tends to send most tokens to a few favorite experts because those experts get more gradient signal and become even more attractive, a rich-get-richer effect. To fix this, each expert is given a capacity limit on how many tokens it can process per batch, and tokens beyond that are dropped or passed through unchanged. There's also an auxiliary loss added during training that encourages the router to spread tokens more evenly across experts. MoE models also seem to need more training data than dense models to reach their full potential.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct qualitative picture of collapse, capacity, and the data-hungry claim, but no formula for the aux loss, no mechanism for why more data is needed, no scaling exponent language.

hire.answer: Routing collapse is a positive feedback loop: an expert that gets slightly more tokens gets more gradient updates, improves faster, and the router learns to send it even more tokens, until a few experts absorb most traffic and the rest are undertrained. To bound this, each expert has a capacity C = capacity_factor * (tokens_per_batch / E); tokens routed to an already-full expert are dropped (skip that layer, residual-only) or, in some implementations, overflow to a second-choice expert. The auxiliary load-balancing loss (Switch Transformer style) is aux_loss = E * sum_i (f_i * P_i), where f_i is the fraction of tokens actually dispatched to expert i and P_i is the router's average softmax probability for expert i; this product is minimized when both are close to uniform (1/E), and it's added to the main loss with a small coefficient. On data-hunger: because routing is imperfect and capacity-limited, each expert effectively sees a noisier, smaller, and less i.i.d. slice of the data than a dense FFN of the same size would see across all tokens, so MoE needs more total tokens to fully specialize its experts and reach the loss a dense-FLOP-equivalent model would reach -- empirically this shows up as MoE scaling laws having a different (typically less favorable per active-parameter) data exponent than dense scaling laws.
hire.interviewer_note: Correct feedback-loop mechanism, correct capacity formula, correct (or close) aux loss form, and a real mechanism for the data-hunger effect. Strong.

strong_hire.answer: Routing collapse mechanism: the router's softmax scores are trained jointly with expert usefulness, so any early asymmetry (initialization noise) creates a rich-get-richer loop -- experts favored early get more gradient signal, become better, and get favored more, converging to using only a handful of the E experts, wasting the extra total-parameter capacity you paid for. Mitigations, in order of maturity: (1) capacity factor c bounds tokens per expert per batch to C = c * tokens_per_batch / E (c typically 1.0-1.25 at train time, higher at inference); tokens that exceed capacity for their top choice are dropped (that token's residual stream skips the expert FFN entirely for that layer) or spill to their next-best expert, both of which directly hurt quality on the dropped tokens, so drop rate is itself a monitored training health metric. (2) the Switch Transformer auxiliary loss L_aux = alpha * E * sum_{i=1}^{E} f_i * P_i where f_i = (1/T) * sum_t 1[token t routed to expert i] (a hard, non-differentiable load fraction) and P_i = (1/T) * sum_t p_i(t) (the differentiable mean router probability for expert i); the product f_i * P_i is minimized at uniform 1/E and provides gradient signal through P_i even though f_i itself is not differentiable, with alpha typically ~1e-2. (3) Newer loss-free approaches (DeepSeek-V2/V3) add a learned per-expert bias updated by a separate control rule (increase bias for underused experts, decrease for overused) so the primary loss doesn't have to trade off against balance at all, avoiding the quality tax that a nonzero aux-loss coefficient imposes. On the data-scaling exponent: dense scaling laws (Chinchilla) fit L(N,D) = E + A/N^a + B/D^b with a and b calibrated for dense FFNs where every parameter sees every token's gradient. In MoE, active parameters see only the tokens routed to them, and capacity limits plus imperfect routing mean the effective number of gradient updates per expert-parameter, for a fixed global token budget D, is lower and noisier than the dense case -- so to reach the same per-active-parameter loss, MoE needs proportionally more tokens, i.e. its fitted b exponent (and/or the D-term coefficient) differs from the dense fit, and several MoE scaling studies (e.g. DeepSeek's and Google's MoE scaling-law papers) explicitly report a different, more data-hungry optimal tokens-per-active-parameter ratio than the dense ~20:1 Chinchilla figure, often needing substantially more tokens per active parameter to close the gap with a comparable dense model. Practically this means naively applying the dense 20:1 heuristic to size MoE training runs under-trains them relative to their true compute-optimal point, and I'd re-derive N_opt/D_opt via an MoE-specific IsoFLOP sweep rather than reuse dense constants.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Precise aux-loss formula with differentiability caveat, names the loss-free bias alternative (DeepSeek), and gives the actual mechanistic argument for why the fitted scaling exponent differs plus the practical consequence for run sizing. Principal/research-lead depth.

questions.title: The data wall and deriving the scaling law from IsoFLOP minima
questions.prompt: Derive the parametric loss law L(N, D) = E + A/N^a + B/D^b from the IsoFLOP methodology, and explain what the 'data wall' means for extrapolating it forward.
probes: What does the irreducible term E represent, and why can't training remove it?
If you're data-constrained (fixed D, growing compute), what does the law say you should do with N?
criteria: IsoFLOP: fix C=6ND, sweep N (so D=C/6N), fit loss vs N per budget, take minima
three additive terms: irreducible entropy E, finite-N approximation error A/N^a, finite-D approximation error B/D^b
minima across C values fit N_opt(C) ~ C^alpha, D_opt(C) ~ C^beta with alpha+beta~1
data wall: D_opt keeps growing with C but real high-quality text data is finite -> D becomes the binding constraint, not compute

consequence: past the wall, increasing N alone still improves loss slower (A/N^a term) while B/D^b term stalls, motivating data-efficiency techniques (repeated epochs, synthetic data, quality filtering)

no_hire.answer: The loss formula just says a bigger model with more data gets a lower loss, and the data wall means eventually you run out of internet text to train on.
no_hire.interviewer_note: No derivation, no functional form, no explanation of why each term exists.

weak_hire.answer: You run training jobs at several fixed compute budgets, and at each budget try different model sizes, plotting loss against model size. The best point at each budget gives you the compute-optimal N and D. Fitting these across budgets gives a power-law formula for loss in terms of N and D, with a term that never goes away no matter how big N and D get. The data wall is the idea that we're running out of the highest-quality training text on the internet, so future models may become bottlenecked by data rather than compute.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct high-level IsoFLOP description and correct qualitative data-wall framing, but never writes down the actual functional form L=E+A/N^a+B/D^b or explains why three terms with those specific meanings.

hire.answer: IsoFLOP procedure: for several fixed C, train models across a range of N (with D=C/(6N) implied), plot final loss against N, and fit a parabola (or similar smooth curve) to find the loss-minimizing N* at that C, giving paired (N*, D*) per budget. Fitting a power law to how N* and D* grow with C across budgets gives N_opt(C) ~ C^alpha, D_opt(C) ~ C^beta, and substituting back gives the parametric form L(N,D) = E + A/N^a + B/D^b: E is the irreducible entropy of natural text (the loss of an ideal predictor that still can't remove real-world randomness/ambiguity), A/N^a captures the approximation error from finite model capacity, and B/D^b captures the estimation error from finite training data (not having seen enough examples to learn the true distribution). The data wall refers to D_opt growing with compute under this law, but the supply of unique, high-quality natural language text being finite, so at some compute scale the optimal D from the formula exceeds what actually exists, forcing a departure from the compute-optimal N:D ratio.
hire.interviewer_note: Correct derivation sketch, correct meaning of each of the three terms, and correct statement of the data-wall constraint. Strong.

strong_hire.answer: Derivation: hold C = 6ND fixed (the standard training FLOPs approximation for a dense transformer), so D = C/(6N) and every point on an IsoFLOP curve is parameterized purely by N. Train models across a grid of N per fixed C, plot final training loss against N, and fit a local quadratic (Chinchilla's approach 2) to each IsoFLOP curve to read off the minimizing N*(C) and corresponding D*(C)=C/(6N*(C)). Repeating across many C and fitting power laws to the minima gives N*(C) ~ C^alpha and D*(C) ~ C^beta, empirically alpha ~ beta ~ 0.5, i.e. both should scale roughly with the square root of compute. Substituting these fits back through the loss-vs-N curves at each C and generalizing off the optimal frontier gives the two-dimensional parametric law L(N,D) = E + A/N^a + B/D^b, a sum of three independent error sources: E is the entropy of natural language itself (the best any model could do, since some tokens are genuinely unpredictable -- no amount of N or D removes this, it's a floor, not a bias/variance term); A/N^a is a finite-capacity/approximation-error term (even with infinite data, a model of finite width can't represent the true conditional distribution exactly, and this error shrinks as a power law in N); B/D^b is a finite-sample/estimation-error term (even with infinite capacity, a model trained on finite D hasn't seen enough of the distribution to pin down its parameters exactly). Minimizing L subject to C=6ND via Lagrange multipliers recovers exactly the N*(C) ~ C^0.5, D*(C) ~ C^0.5 result, closing the loop between the parametric law and the IsoFLOP-fit exponents. The data wall: because D*(C) grows as C^0.5 under compute-optimal allocation, every 100x increase in compute compute-optimally demands ~10x more unique training tokens; but the stock of unique high-quality natural text (filtered common-crawl-scale corpora, books, code, etc.) is finite and estimated in the tens of trillions of tokens, a ceiling current frontier runs are already approaching. Past that ceiling the B/D^b term stops improving (D can't grow further without quality-degrading repetition, whose marginal value decays -- repeated epochs behave like a discounted fraction of fresh tokens) while A/N^a still has room to improve with more N, so the compute-optimal allocation implied by the clean law breaks down: you either accept multi-epoch training with diminishing per-token value, pursue synthetic/generated data to expand D artificially, over-invest in N beyond the naive Chinchilla ratio to spend surplus compute somewhere it still helps, or shift compute into inference-time methods (search, tool use) that don't require more pretraining tokens at all. This is the live strategic tension frontier labs face once D approaches its ceiling.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Full Lagrangian closing-the-loop derivation connecting IsoFLOP exponents back to the parametric law, precise statistical meaning of each term (entropy floor vs approximation vs estimation error), quantitative data-wall consequence (100x compute needs 10x tokens), and concrete strategic responses (synthetic data, epoching diminishing returns, inference-time compute shift). Research-lead/principal depth.
